gaps.construct: return (clamped value, ErrRange): a failure that also delivers a usable result
gaps.description: Scribe failures are bare names with no payload and an operation either gives back or fails. The clamped value is carried in an invented failure payload (`fail with RangeError with nearest_value X`, read as `nearest_value of problem`).

gaps.construct: err from ParseUint is inspected, ErrRange is tolerated and execution continues with the returned value
gaps.description: Recovering a value from a failure and continuing needs `set` inside an `on failure` line; the doc only says such a line must give back, fail or call something, so assigning there is not clearly allowed.

gaps.construct: s[0] compared with rune literals '+' and '-'; s = s[1:]
gaps.description: No character or byte type, no character literal and no substring/slice form in the doc. `item 0 of text` compared with one-letter Text and `part of text from 1 until count of text` are invented.
No shift operator and no exponent operator; `2 to the power (size - 1)` is invented.

gaps.construct: int64, uint64, uint(...), int64(...) casts and a run-time bitSize choosing the width
gaps.description: The doc has Int and Nat with no sized integers and no explicit conversion syntax; conversions go through a declared helper `int_from`. The bit width is a runtime parameter in Go, which a refinement type cannot express directly, so the result type is plain Int with the range enforced only by the body.

gaps.construct: -int64(cutoff) where cutoff is 2^63 relies on two's-complement wrap to yield MinInt64
gaps.description: The doc promises checked arithmetic but never says whether Int is bounded; if Int is 64-bit, `0 - int_from cutoff` would fail at int_from for size 64; if unbounded, it is exact. The doc does not settle which.
Top-level `let` appears in example 17 but nothing says how a binding that depends on the compilation target is written.
The doc never shows unary minus or the literals true and false; `0 - x`, `true` and `false` are assumed.

doc_rules_contradicted: An `on failure` line may not be empty: it must give back a value, fail, or call something. (the RangeError handler only sets a variable)
invented_syntax: fail with RangeError with nearest_value X
nearest_value of problem (reading a failure payload)
on failure RangeError as problem (binding a single named failure; the doc shows `as` only after an `or` list)
item 0 of text compared with "+" (character access on Text)
part of text from 1 until count of text
notes: Go's (value, error) convention where both are meaningful is common in parsing and I/O code (e.g. partial reads), and Scribe's either-give-back-or-fail model has no room for it; failures with payloads would cover most cases. Sized integer types and explicit casts are absent, which matters for any parser or wire-format code. Text is treated as opaque, so even a one-character prefix check needs invented syntax.
